primary.title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
primary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. METHODS: We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. RESULTS: SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. INTERPRETATION: We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. primary.title: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
primary.abstract: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.

primary.title: The IKC-leptin axis functions as a molecular bridge between neurodevelopment and endocrine signaling.
primary.abstract: Kcnb1-null mice exhibit hypoleptinemia, disrupted Kcnb1-integrin-K+ channel complex (IKC) interactions with the leptin receptor (LepR) in proopiomelanocortin neurons, and broad neurodevelopmental and cognitive abnormalities. Because leptin is neurotrophic and IKC-LepR assemblies are present in neocortex, we tested whether leptin modifies these phenotypes. Early-life leptin supplementation partially improved behavioral and cognitive deficits and more strongly corrected anatomical and neuronal abnormalities. In null cortical neurons, leptin normalized dendritic overgrowth and F-actin dynamics through LepR- and integrin-dependent mechanisms. WT animals and neurons showed modest leptin responses; however, integrin manipulation unmasked leptin sensitivity, whereas LepR blockade induced null-like defects without exogenous leptin. These findings support a dual-mode model in which LepR signaling is regulated by both ligand availability and IKC-dependent mechanisms, identifying IKC-LepR coupling as a molecular interface linking endocrine signaling to neocortical development.

primary.title: Striatal 6-hydroxydopamine lesion in rats induces dysregulation of the gut barrier.
primary.abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is a well-recognized prodromal feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the mechanisms linking central dopaminergic (DA) neurodegeneration to gut pathology remain unclear. Previous studies have reported intestinal permeability and microbiome changes in toxin-based PD models, but the specific contribution of nigrostriatal injury to these outcomes is unknown. Here, we used the 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) rat model to determine whether selective loss of substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) DA neurons disrupt gut barrier integrity and microbial homeostasis. Neurodegeneration was confirmed by progressive apomorphine-induced rotations and reduced tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression in the SNc and Dorsal Lateral Striatum (DLS). 6-OHDA lesioning led to increased circulating lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (iFABP), consistent with impaired gut barrier function. Immunostaining for Villin, an actin-binding protein in microvilli, revealed no changes to the enterocyte brush border in either the ileum or colon. However, the tight junction protein zona occludens-1 (ZO-1) had marked reductions in both the ileum and more profoundly in the colon, indicating regional vulnerability. 6-OHDA-lesioned rats also exhibited alterations in specific gram-negative bacterial classes and reduced short-chain fatty acid levels (SCFAs). Together, these findings demonstrate that neurotrauma in the DA system can compromise gut integrity and microbial composition, supporting a brain-to-gut axis in PD pathophysiology and identifying gut barrier protection as a potential therapeutic target.

primary.title: The PINK1-VCP-p47 pathway protects against tau-induced dendritic shrinkage in cortical neurons through interaction with STIP1.
primary.abstract: Microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) contributes to the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and some forms of Frontotemporal Lobar Dementia wherein dendritic simplification is strongly related to cognitive dysfunction. Loss of function mutations in PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) cause recessive early-onset Parkinson's disease with dementia, and reduced wild-type PINK1 expression is observed in sporadic AD. We previously found that PINK1 interacts with valosin-containing protein (VCP) and promotes phosphorylation of the VCP co-factor NSFL1C (p47). This study was designed to test the hypothesis that PINK1 rescues tau-induced dendritic simplification through the VCP-p47 pathway, and to define neuroprotective mechanisms downstream of p47 phosphorylation. Mouse primary cortical neurons were transfected with 2N4R-Tau and plasmids encoding components of the PINK1-VCP-p47 signaling pathway and the impact on tau-mediated dendritic injury was assessed. Immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry, immunoblotting, RNAi and Sholl analysis were performed to define downstream mechanisms of neuroprotection. Tau-induced dendritic shortening and simplification was fully rescued by co-expression of PINK1, VCP, p47 or the p47-S176D phosphomimic (p47D), but not by the non-phosphorylatable p47-S176A (p47A) variant. Pathway analysis showed enhanced interactions of p47D with proteins in the Rho-GTPase pathway. Immunoprecipitation confirmed that STIP1 interacts with p47D to a significantly higher degree than p47A. Overexpression of STIP1 rescued tau-mediated dendritic simplification. Moreover, STIP1 siRNA impaired the neuroprotective effects of both PINK1 and p47D, indicating an essential role in the PINK1-p47D neuroprotection pathway. The current study highlights a novel PINK1-(phospho)p47-STIP1 signaling axis that promotes dendritic complexity and protects against tau-induced neurodegeneration in cortical neurons.

primary.title: Nuclear distribution element-like 1 is associated with dentate gyrus remodeling after status epilepticus in a pilocarpine-induced mouse model.
primary.abstract: Structural remodeling of the dentate gyrus is a hallmark of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Nuclear distribution element-like 1 (Ndel1), a cytoskeleton-associated protein involved in neuronal migration and dendritic development, has not been characterized in dentate gyrus remodeling during epileptogenesis. Here, we investigated region- and cell-type-specific alterations in Ndel1 expression in a pilocarpine-induced mouse model of TLE and examined the effects of adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated Ndel1 expression on structural remodeling. Immunofluorescence was used to define Ndel1 localization across neural stem cells, granule lineage cells, mature neurons, and astrocytes, and dendritic architecture was assessed using Golgi staining and Sholl analysis. Total hippocampal Ndel1 expression increased after status epilepticus, whereas Ndel1-positive cells decreased selectively in the subgranular zone but increased among granule lineage cells in the hilus. Ndel1 was preferentially expressed in BLBP-positive neural stem cells and mature neurons, but not in neuroblasts. Activated astrocytic processes exhibited increased spatial association with Ndel1-positive cells during early remodeling. Ndel1 overexpression was associated with partial normalization of neuronal marker distribution, increased dendritic spine density, and reduced dendritic branching complexity. These findings suggest that Ndel1 is associated with region- and lineage-specific structural remodeling in the dentate gyrus during epileptogenesis.

primary.title: Pre- and post-stroke memantine administration attenuates neurological deficits, infarct size, and astrogliosis, with a concomitant increase in MAP2 protein in a rat stroke model.
primary.abstract: Over the past 30 years, the global incidence of stroke and related disability-adjusted life years has risen significantly, underscoring the urgent need for effective therapeutic strategies. Memantine (Mem), a non-competitive antagonist of N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptors, has been investigated as a potential treatment in stroke models. By blocking NMDA receptor activity, Mem can prevent excessive calcium influx and excitotoxic neuronal death, thereby promoting neuroprotection with good tolerability. Because early intervention is crucial, we evaluated a sequential memantine regimen in 32 male Sprague-Dawley rats (300-350 g). A low dose of Mem (0.2 mg/kg) was administered before permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (pMCAO), followed by a higher dose (10 mg/kg) two hours after occlusion. Neurological function was evaluated 24 h later using the modified Neurological Severity Score (mNSS). Brain tissue was collected for immunohistochemical analysis of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2) near the infarct area. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) measured brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD95). Memantine treatment preserved neurological function, reduced infarct size, and decreased GFAP levels, indicating diminished astrocyte reactivity. Additionally, MAP2 presence increased compared to the untreated pMCAO group, suggesting neuronal preservation. No significant changes were observed in BDNF or PSD95 levels. Memantine administered before and after stroke minimized tissue loss and prevented early astrogliosis, while preserving neuronal structural integrity as indicated by MAP2. In contrast, no immediate changes were detected in BDNF or PSD95, implying that memantine-induced neuroprotection occurs before the appearance of plasticity-related molecular adaptations in the early post-stroke period.

secondary.title: Proteomic Mapping of Novel Tubulin Post-Translational Modifications in Trypanosoma cruzi Cytoskeleton.
secondary.abstract: Microtubules play central roles in the organization and morphology of trypanosomatid parasites, forming highly specialized cytoskeletal structures such as the subpellicular corset, the flagellar axoneme, and the mitotic spindle. Functional specialization of MTs is proposed to be regulated by the "tubulin code", which is defined by the combination of different α- and β-tubulin isotypes, a set of post-translational modifications and specific MT-binding proteins. Although multiple tubulin post-translational modifications have been described in trypanosomatids using specific antibodies or mass spectrometry, to date no comprehensive mapping has been reported in Trypanosoma cruzi, the causative agent of Chagas Disease. In the present work, we performed a high-resolution proteomic analysis of PTMs present in α- and β-tubulin subunits of the T. cruzi Dm28c strain, using tubulin-enriched extracts obtained by in vitro polymerization. Multiple high-confidence PTMs were identified by LC-MS/MS, including acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, and polyglutamylation, for which many modified amino acids had not been previously reported in trypanosomatids. Structural mapping of these modifications onto a predicted α/β-tubulin heterodimer showed that most modified residues are located in solvent-exposed regions of the protein. Together, these findings provide the first high-confidence proteomic landscape of tubulin PTMs in T. cruzi and support the existence of a complex tubulin code contributing to microtubule regulation in this parasite.

secondary.title: α-Catenin phosphorylation is tension-sensitive and supports epithelial barrier functions via afadin.
secondary.abstract: Zonula adherens junctions (zAJs) are spatially proximal to tight junctions (TJs), in a superstructure known as the apical junctional complex (AJC). A key component of the AJC is a circumferential ring of F-actin, but how actomyosin contractility drives AJC structure and epithelial barrier function is incompletely understood. Here, we show that a central mechanosensitive component of zAJ, α-catenin (α-cat), undergoes force-dependent phosphorylation in an unstructured linker region. This modification in turn primes the α-cat middle region for effector binding. We credential afadin, a TJ/AJ scaffold protein, as a mechanochemical binding partner of α-cat, identifying residues in α-cat required for binding. α-Cat phosphorylation and afadin binding support their co-enrichment at zAJ and barrier function. A mouse model that prevents α-cat phosphorylation is particularly detrimental to postnatal brain development, leading to hydrocephalus with junctional features similar to an afadin-binding mutant form of α-cat. These data support a model where α-cat integrates mechanical and chemical signals to progressively promote zAJ enrichment, effector recruitment, and barrier function.

secondary.title: Non-muscle actinopathy-associated loss-of-function actin variants modulate cytoskeletal reorganization.
secondary.abstract: Variants in ACTB gene encoding for cytoplasmic β-actin result in a group of rare disorders called non-muscle actinopathies (NMA). A subgroup of NMA patients with ACTB pLoF (predicted loss-of-function) disorder have various congenital malformations, such as microcephaly and intellectual disability. We investigated the cellular effects of an ACTB pLoF missense variant, G302A, and a four-amino-acid deletion, S338-I341 in cytoskeletal β-actin, in patient-derived fibroblast cells. We found that neither of the mutations affected the organization of actin or the width of the actin-filament bundles, while the mutation G302A reduced the stiffness of the cells as measured by using atomic force microscopy. The latter effect might be associated with the misorganization of tubulin and with the increased size and number of focal adhesions. When we challenged the cells by monolayer stretching and followed the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, we found that G302A mutant cells showed denser actin filament bundles within the cells compared to wild type cells. At the same time, the extent of cofilin reorganization from the cell periphery was increased upon stretch, and this correlated with an increased cofilin phosphorylation. In the case of deletion, while the extent of cofilin phosphorylation increased, the extent of reorganization was unaltered; rather, the phosphorylation of myosin light chain, important in counteracting external force, was reduced by 75%. We could partially rescue this effect by overexpressing the active form of the formin mDia1. Our findings open the possibility to verify the cellular phenotype in the most affected patients' cells, in neurons.

secondary.title: A PTPRO inhibitor Pi mitigates endotoxemia-induced encephalopathy-mediated blood-brain barrier disruption through cytoskeletal regulation.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Septic encephalopathy (SE) is closely associated with disruption of blood-brain barrier (BBB), resulting in neurological deficits and poor clinical outcomes. Protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) regulates disease states by dephosphorylating membrane-associated proteins and modulating intracellular signalling. Here we have examined the role of PTPRO in regulating BBB permeability and have assessed a PTPRO inhibitor (Pi) in mitigating BBB disruption during endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Genetic and pharmacological approaches, including PTPRO overexpression, knockdown or deficiency and Pi treatment, were used to evaluate endothelial dysfunction in bEND.3 cells, primary mouse brain microvascular endothelial cells and an LPS-induced murine model of endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. Barrier dysfunction, cytoskeletal remodelling and signalling events were assessed using permeability assays, immunoblotting, immunofluorescence and in vivo BBB leakage analyses. KEY RESULTS: LPS increased PTPRO expression in brain tissue from endotoxemic mice and cerebral endothelial cells. Elevated PTPRO promoted F-actin reorganization, stress fibre formation and intercellular gap formation, whereas Pi treatment or PTPRO silencing attenuated these changes. PTPRO overexpression worsened endothelial barrier dysfunction, while Pi reduced thrombin-induced permeability in bEND.3 cells and wild-type primary endothelial cells. Primary endothelial cells from PTPRO-deficient mice were protected. Mechanistically, PTPRO regulated cytoskeletal dynamics through the ErbB2-Rho-MLC2 pathway. In vivo, Pi treatment and PTPRO deficiency reduced BBB leakage, with limited effects on inflammatory cytokines. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: These findings identify PTPRO as an important regulator of BBB disruption in endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy and support pharmacological targeting of PTPRO as a potential strategy for preserving sepsis-associated BBB injury.

secondary.title: Neurofilament transport kinetics can be explained by the activity of small numbers of independent kinesin and dynein motors.
secondary.abstract: Neurofilaments, which are intermediate filaments, are long flexible protein polymers that are transported bidirectionally along microtubule tracks in axons. Kymograph analysis of neurofilaments has revealed rapid intermittent movement with average run lengths consistent with the processive bouts of single motors, and frequent pauses and reversals that suggest rapid switching between opposing motors. To explore this, we used discrete stochastic models of kinesin and dynein motors to simulate neurofilament movement by teams of independent motors in axons. We describe an unbiased automated sampling algorithm to identify the numbers of kinesin and dynein motors required to match the range of pause times, run times, run lengths, and velocities for neurofilaments in a large data set of ∼37,000 runs and pauses acquired with 30.3 ms resolution. We find that the diverse kinetic behavior of neurofilaments can be explained by the activity of 1-2 kinesin or dynein motors, which interact indirectly via the mechanical forces they exert on the neurofilament cargo. Simultaneous engagement of opposing motors was rare in our simulations, indicating that the motile behavior can be explained by alternating kinesin and dynein activity without a competition between motors of opposite directionality.

secondary.title: PIST couples actin cytoskeleton dynamics through a WH2-like actin-binding domain.
secondary.abstract: Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellar cortex require tight coordination between receptor trafficking and cytoskeletal remodeling to sustain synaptogenesis, structural plasticity, and motor learning. The glutamate δ2 receptor (GluRδ2), a hallmark component of parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses, depends on intracellular scaffolding proteins for proper localization and signaling. PIST (GOPC), a neuronal PDZ domain-containing protein originally identified as a selective GluRδ2-interacting partner, has emerged as an important regulator of receptor trafficking and synaptic organization. Here, we reveal a previously unrecognized biochemical function of PIST as an actin-binding protein. Biochemical and cellular analyses show that PIST directly associates with filamentous actin in a concentration-dependent manner, suppresses actin polymerization in vitro, and co-localizes with actin in neuronal cells. Mechanistically, this interaction is mediated by a WH2-like motif within PIST. PIST may function as a molecular link between the actin cytoskeleton and the protein trafficking machinery, suggesting a potential new mechanism underlying the coordinated regulation of receptor transport and synaptic structural plasticity in neurons.

secondary.title: Distribution of doublecortin in the developing retina of birds: A comparative analysis.
secondary.abstract: The avian retina presents an elegant and highly accessible model for investigating the spatial and temporal dynamics of neurogenesis within the central nervous system. In recent years, the microtubule cytoskeleton has emerged not merely as a structural scaffold, but as a dynamic regulator of the transition of a morphologically homogeneous pool of multipotent progenitor cells to postmitotic neurons. Doublecortin (DCX) is a microtubule-associated protein broadly recognized for its fundamental roles in neuronal migration, differentiation, and structural plasticity within the developing nervous system. While its roles in the brain are well-documented, the precise spatiotemporal distribution of DCX in the developing retina of birds remains poorly understood. In this study we investigated the expression pattern of DCX during embryonic development of the retina of one altricial (zebra finch, Taeniopygia guttata) and two precocial (chicken, Gallus gallus; Japanese quail, Coturnix coturnix) bird species using immunohistochemical techniques. Our results demonstrated that the onset of DCX expression coincided chronotopographically with the onset of neurogenesis in the developing retina. In these early stages, DCX expression is tightly colocalized with the neuronal marker class III β-tubulin. As retinal histogenesis progressed to more advanced stages, DCX expression persisted and segregated into specific subsets of ganglion, amacrine, and horizontal cells. Furthermore, prominent immunoreactivity was maintained within the ciliary marginal zone (CMZ), highlighting its association with late-stage retinal progenitors and ongoing neurogenesis. These findings reveal a conserved spatiotemporal expression pattern of DCX across diverse avian species. Furthermore, it suggests that some elements of the cytoskeleton and its associated regulatory proteins form a functional continuous biological continuum: first acting as drivers of neurogenesis and migration and, subsequently, transitioning into structural stabilizers that lock in and maintain the complex morphology of fully differentiated, mature retinal neurons.

secondary.title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
secondary.abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

secondary.title: HSV-1 induces stable associations between the Golgi and endosomes within the cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment of neuronal cells.
secondary.abstract: Assembly of mature herpesvirus particles is associated with extensive rearrangement of cytoplasmic membranes. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection in neuronal cells induces the formation of a distinctive cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment (cVAC), in which rearranged host membranes and viral proteins are clustered at the perinuclear microtubule-organizing center (MTOC). Although both the trans-Golgi network (TGN) and endosomal compartments have been implicated as membrane sources for cytoplasmic envelopment, how secretory and endosomal pathways are reorganized and associated within the cVAC remains unclear. Here, we treated HSV-1-infected cells with nocodazole at a post-entry stage to disperse membrane components of the cVAC and identify microtubule-independent membrane organizations and associations using immunofluorescence imaging. We found that the Golgi apparatus was fragmented during infection but maintained cisternal stacking, as the Golgi markers GM130, GalT, and GRASP65 remained colocalized in both the absence and presence of nocodazole. We further demonstrated that Golgi mini-stacks retained their association with Rab6 during HSV-1 infection and formed microtubule-independent associations with early and recycling endosomes, resulting in the formation of Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks. Viral capsid, glycoprotein, and tegument proteins were colocalized with Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks in both the presence and absence of microtubules, suggesting that this membrane complex serves as a site of cytoplasmic envelopment regardless of clustering at the MTOC. Formation of these stable Golgi-endosome associations did not require viral capsids. Neither actin filaments nor acetylated microtubules colocalized with Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks, suggesting that cytoskeletal elements are not required for this association.IMPORTANCEMany viruses remodel host cytoplasmic membranes to facilitate their assembly. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying this remodeling may reveal novel antiviral targets while also providing insight into fundamental principles of intracellular membrane organization. Infection with an important human pathogen, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), induces extensive membrane remodeling that leads to the formation of the cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment (cVAC) in neuronal cells, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that HSV-1 induces stable associations between membranes within the cVAC. Our findings support a model in which HSV-1 generates a dynamic hybrid membrane compartment during infection, potentially reconciling conflicting views on the roles of distinct membrane sources in cytoplasmic assembly.

secondary.title: Hydrogel-mediated local PTK2 inhibition promotes ordered axonal regeneration associated with cytoskeletal remodeling after spinal cord injury.
secondary.abstract: Disorganized axonal regrowth after spinal cord injury (SCI) may compromise the spatial organization and directional alignment of regenerating axons. Our previous COL6-modified hydrogel model revealed physical guidance-independent, self-organized spinal cord regeneration, whose neuron-intrinsic mechanisms remain unclear. Using proteomic screening of a COL6-modified hydrogel model that promotes ordered spinal cord regeneration, we identified protein tyrosine kinase 2 (PTK2) as a candidate intracellular regulator associated with axonal organization. In vitro, PTK2 downregulation by siRNA or pharmacological inhibition with PF-573228 reduced neurite tortuosity and branching and increased radial directional coherence. Exploratory long-read transcriptomic analysis, together with Western blotting, revealed coordinated changes in integrin-, RhoA-, cofilin-, and actin-related signaling after PTK2 inhibition, consistent with cytoskeleton-associated remodeling. To achieve localized PTK2 inhibition in vivo, PF-573228 was incorporated into an injectable thiol-modified hyaluronan/gelatin hydrogel, termed HaG-PF, which exhibited porous microarchitecture and hyaluronidase responsiveness. In a mouse model of complete spinal cord transection, HaG-PF was associated with reduced p-PTK2 at the 4-week endpoint, increased NF200+ axonal presence, improved two- and three-dimensional axonal organization, increased CGRP+ fibers within the lesion site, and the presence of 5-HT+ fibers in the caudal stump. Improved axonal organization was accompanied by enhanced locomotor and electrophysiological recovery. Collectively, these findings identify local PTK2 inhibition as a molecular strategy for promoting more organized axonal regeneration after SCI.

secondary.title: Transcriptomic analysis reveals distinct expression patterns in focal cortical dysplasia.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a common cause of drug-resistant epilepsy in children and adults and exhibits substantial clinical and histopathological heterogeneity. However, morphological classification alone does not fully explain variability in epileptogenicity, disease severity, or treatment response. METHODS: We aimed to define molecular mechanisms underlying FCD heterogeneity using integrated transcriptomic and regulatory analyses. RNA and small RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) were conducted on cortical tissue resected during epilepsy surgery from 66 patients with histopathologically confirmed FCD subtypes IA (n = 17), IIA (n = 25), and IIB (n = 24), along with 15 postmortem cortical control samples. Differential expression and weighted gene coexpression network analysis were used to identify coordinated transcriptional programs, and microRNA (miRNA) profiling was integrated to assess posttranscriptional regulatory mechanisms. Integrative multivariate analyses (DIABLO and sparse partial least squares discriminant analysis) were used to evaluate subtype discrimination, and findings were validated using an independent RNA-seq dataset. RESULTS: FCD subtypes showed distinct but partially overlapping molecular profiles. FCD IA showed a comparatively subtle transcriptional profile, dominated by reduced expression of genes involved in cortical development, neuronal signaling, ion regulation, and metabolic stress. FCD IIA displayed a modest yet coherent molecular signature involving developmental and neuronal disruption, together with metabolic stress and autophagy. FCD IIB exhibited the most extensive transcriptional remodeling, including activation of antigen presentation pathways, complement activation, cytoskeleton reorganization, synaptic alterations, and extracellular matrix organization. Differential miRNA profiling identified shared miRNAs, including miR-320 family, miR-27a-5p, miR-142-5p, and miR-21-5p, alongside subtype-specific regulatory patterns. Integration of messenger RNA and miRNA data revealed concordant alterations, indicating that miRNA dysregulation may contribute to stabilization of subtype-specific transcriptional states. SIGNIFICANCE: These findings demonstrate that FCD is characterized by coordinated transcriptional and posttranscriptional network alterations that extend beyond morphological classification and may contribute to variability in epileptogenicity across subtypes.

secondary.title: Functionalized Silica-Coated Metallic Replicas of Intracellular Protein Assemblies.
secondary.abstract: To replicate hierarchical biological architectures, biotemplating leverages diverse biological structures as templates for inorganic materials. Among the various inorganic materials explored in biotemplating, silica is an attractive material because of its stability and biocompatibility. However, existing biotemplating methods are largely nonselective, yielding silica replicas of bulk biological specimens. Here, we report an approach for selective materialization of targeted protein-associated architectures from cells and tissue slices, enabling recovery of the resulting silicified structures after enzymatic removal of surrounding non-target biomolecular components. To this end, we (i) immunolabeled target proteins with fluorophore-conjugated antibodies, (ii) embedded specimens in a hydrogel, (iii) removed endogenous proteins via enzymatic digestion, and (iv) converted the retained fluorophore patterns into Au nanoparticle assemblies through fluorophore-directed nanogold labeling and electroless Au growth, followed by silica coating. Using this strategy, we fabricated microtubule-derived silica bioreplicas from a human immune-lineage cell line and tuned their overall size by adjusting the expansion of the surrounding hydrogel matrix. Furthermore, functionalization of the silica surface with magnetic nanoparticles enables controlled motion of the bioreplicas under electromagnetic actuation. Finally, we extended the method to mouse brain slices and produced thermally stable silica bioreplicas of astrocytic and oligodendrocytic structures. Overall, this work expands the structural diversity and selectivity of silica-based biomimetic materials and broadens the palette of biotemplating templates.

secondary.title: The neuroprotective mechanism of baicalein related to mitophagy mediated by MAPK1/RSK1 in a murine model of Parkinson's disease.
secondary.abstract: UNLABELLED: This study aims to investigate the neuroprotective effects and underlying molecular mechanisms of baicalein (Bai) in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease (PD) induced by 1-Methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP). Using an MPTP-induced PD mouse model, the effects of Bai intraperitoneal injection on motor function and dopaminergic neuronal injury were assessed. Adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9)-mediated mitogen-activated protein kinase 1 overexpression (oe-MAPK1) was employed for gain-of-function experiments. Western blot technique was adopted to measure the levels of MAPK1, ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (RSK1), phosphorylated RSK1, PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1), Parkin, microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3)-II/I, and p62. Additionally, mitochondrial membrane potential and mitochondrial ultrastructure were observed to assess mitochondrial function. The binding between Bai and MAPK1 was examined using molecular docking and cellular thermal shift assay. Bai intraperitoneal injection markedly alleviated motor deficits, mitigated dopaminergic neuronal loss, raised mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduced ultrastructural mitochondrial damage post MPTP-induced PD in mice. Meanwhile, Bai upregulated PINK1, Parkin, and the LC3-II/I ratio while downregulating p62, indicating enhanced mitophagy. With a binding energy of -7.8 kcal/mol, Bai could directly bind to MAPK1, which destabilized MAPK1 thermostability and suppressed MAPK1 expression as well as subsequent RSK1 phosphorylation. Notably, MAPK1 overexpression repressed mitophagy, aggravated motor dysfunction and neuronal damage, and partially abrogated the neuroprotective efficacy of Bai. Bai binds directly to MAPK1, suppresses the MAPK1/RSK1 signaling cascade, triggers mitophagy, and ultimately ameliorates motor impairment and neuronal degeneration, conferring neuroprotection against PD in mice. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT: Baicalein inhibits the MAPK1 and p-RSK1 signaling pathway in a Parkinson's disease mouse model treated with MPTP. This inhibition activates mitophagy, increases levels of PINK1, Parkin, and the LC3-II/I ratio, while decreasing p62.

secondary.title: Biophysical characterization of Arc protein-RNA interactions.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The activity-regulated cytoskeleton-associated protein (Arc) is essential for synaptic plasticity and memory formation. Arc binds RNA and self-assembles into capsid-like structures reminiscent of retroviral Gag proteins, but the molecular basis of this interaction remains poorly defined. This study sought to characterize the biophysical interactions between Arc protein and its mRNA, focusing on the specificity of mRNA binding and its role in regulating Arc self-assembly. METHODS: Here, we combined biophysical approaches to characterize Arc's RNA binding, assembly behavior, and particle morphology. Transmission electron microscopy was employed to visualize complexes of recombinant human Arc and synthetic Arc mRNA at different mRNA molar ratios. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) quantified RNA-dependent changes in the hydrodynamic size of Arc assemblies, while biolayer interferometry (BLI) determined the binding affinity of Arc for cognate and non-cognate mRNA transcripts. RESULTS: Using recombinant human Arc and synthetic Arc mRNA, we found that RNA binding markedly enlarges Arc complexes. At an optimal mRNA molar ratio of ~1 : 45, Arc forms ~50-nm capsid-like particles, compared with ~30-nm assemblies formed by Arc alone, whereas higher RNA levels promote oversized aggregates. DLS confirmed RNA-dependent particle size growth, and BLI showed that Arc binds its cognate mRNA ~1.5-fold more tightly than a non-cognate transcript. CONCLUSION: The results identify RNA as a crucial cofactor for Arc capsid assembly under physiologically relevant conditions and reveal measurable specificity of Arc for its own mRNA. These findings elucidate how Arc packages its own mRNA, providing insight into Arc-mediated neuronal RNA transfer and advancing the development of Arc-based therapeutic delivery systems.

secondary.title: Microtubule and cytoskeletal destabilization gene expression in the brain vasculature after experimental diffuse traumatic brain injury: Implications for neurodegenerative disease later in life.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative disease risk following traumatic brain injury (TBI) has been associated with vascular abnormalities and brain inflammation. However, the extent to which diffuse TBI with at least one persistent neurological deficit contributes to chronic neurodegeneration is not well understood. In this study, we investigated the impact of experimental diffuse TBI on the cerebral vasculature in the CA1 region of the hippocampus, which is vulnerable to multiple cognitive-associated neurodegenerative diseases. At 6-months post-injury, a timepoint with known cognitive impairment, we employed laser capture microdissection (LCM) to isolate parenchymal blood vessels from the CA1 subregion of the hippocampus in Sprague-Dawley rats subjected to either sham or midline fluid percussion injury. LCM vessels were processed for RNA sequencing and differentially expressed gene (DEG) analyses (DESeq2) were performed, followed by pathway enrichment analysis using genes with a log2FC > 0 and p-value < 0.05. A subset of differentially expressed genes (9%) were associated with microtubule/cytoskeletal organization, including the PLEC gene (encoding plectin) (Log2FC=+9.5, p < 0.0001), a cytoskeletal protein that maintains tissue integrity and whose overexpression has recently been identified as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD). Pathway analyses showed the most upregulated and downregulated biological pathways were involved in neurodegeneration-multiple-diseases (Gene count 11, p-adjusted < 0.01) and AD (Gene count 8, p-adjusted < 0.04). Understanding the complex interplay between TBI, the cerebral vasculature, and neurodegeneration risk is critical for prognosis and interventions that mitigate the long-term effects of brain injury and improve outcomes for patients.

secondary.title: Treadmill exercise rescues cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's mice by repairing axonal mitochondrial transport and synaptic function.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurological disorder characterized by synaptic injury and loss in its early stage. This study aimed to investigate the effects of treadmill exercise on Alzheimer's disease mice, focusing on the related molecular mechanism of axonal transport. METHOD: In this study, 3-month-old male APP/PS1 mice and C57BL/6J mice were used and divided into four groups ( n  = 9). Behavioral performance was evaluated using the Morris water maze, open field test, and tail suspension test. Transmission electron microscopy and ELISA were used to assess the morphology and function of mitochondria and synapses, individually. The colocalization of mitochondria and synapses was analyzed by double-labeling immunofluorescence. Finally, the underlying mechanism of treadmill exercise on Alzheimer's disease mice was evaluated by Western blotting. RESULTS: APP/PS1 mice exhibited significant deficits in spatial learning and memory, accompanied by abnormal ultrastructure and dysfunction in hippocampal mitochondria and synapses. Treadmill exercise could ameliorate cognitive impairments and affective disorders in Alzheimer's disease mice, reduce amyloid-beta levels, improve the morphology and function of mitochondria and synapses, and enhance mitochondrial axonal transport, which might be regulated by the related proteins of kinesins, syntabulin, and dyneins. CONCLUSION: These results suggest that exercise-induced modulation of mitochondrial dynamics can provide neuroprotection and support the development of novel therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer's disease (Video Abstract, SDC 1).

secondary.title: Pathogenic KIF1A variants differentially disrupt axonal trafficking and impede synaptic development.
secondary.abstract: The nervous system relies on billions of neurons connected through trillions of synapses to support vital functions. Despite the importance of this synaptic network, cellular mechanisms dictating synapse formation during human neurodevelopment remain unclear. Long-distance trafficking by the microtubule motor KIF1A is crucial for synaptogenesis and downstream synapse maintenance. Mutations in KIF1A cause KIF1A-associated neurological disorder (KAND). We employed isogenic gene-edited human-induced pluripotent stem cell -derived neurons to assess the effects of disparate pathogenic mutations in KIF1A on synaptic trafficking and function. Null (p.C92*) and hypoactive (p.P305L) mutations delay neurite outgrowth, mislocalize synaptic cargoes, and decrease synapse density. Conversely, a hyperactive (p.R350G) mutation supports neurite outgrowth but causes aberrant motility of synaptic vesicle precursors and deficits in microtubule-dependent presynaptic patterning. Functional analysis of neuronal activity reveals delayed synaptic maturation in loss-of-function mutations (p.P305L, p.C92*) and precocious activity in the hyperactive p.R350G mutation. These data provide insights into how KIF1A mutations with distinct molecular-level impacts lead to significant downstream synaptic deficits in human neurons.

secondary.title: Cofilin 1 overexpression in the ventral hippocampus partially alleviates depressive-like behaviors in postmenopausal depression model mice through the dynamics of dendrites/dendritic spines in relevant brain regions.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The ventral hippocampus (vHPC) itself or its input pathways can directly influence behaviors related to anxiety and depression. Cofilin 1, as a member of the actin-depolymerizing factor/cofilin (ADF/cofilin) family, participates in dendritic spine remodeling, thereby influencing depression-like behaviors. METHODS: To investigate the effects of Cofilin 1 on neural circuits related to depression, this study utilized Thy1-YFP-H transgenic mice to create an ovariectomized (OVX) + chronic restraint stress (CRS)-induced depression model. Recombinant virus AAV2/9 was bilaterally injected into the vHPC CA1 region using stereotactic surgery to knock down or overexpress Cofilin 1. The sucrose preference test (SPT), tail suspension test (TST), elevated plus maze test (EPM), and novel inhibition feeding test (NSFT) were used to assess depression-like behaviors. Meanwhile, ImageJ and Imaris software were employed to analyze the density and morphology of dendrites and dendritic spines of excitatory neurons in the HPC and related brain regions. RESULTS: The results showed that OVX + CRS induced depression-like behaviors in mice. Overexpression of vCA1 Cofilin 1 rescued a subset of depression-like behavioral phenotypes, increased dendritic density in the mPFC and vHPC, and upregulated dendritic spine density in the vHPC CA1 region. It also decreased dendritic density in the aBLA and nucleus accumbens core while increasing dendritic density in the pBLA and AcbSh. These findings suggest that overexpression of vHPC Cofilin 1 may influence depression-related neural structure by altering dendritic and dendritic spine density and connectivity, thereby improving depression-like behaviors. However, although knockdown of vCA1 Cofilin 1 did not significantly affect depression-like behaviors in mice, it reduced dendritic density and overall dendritic spine density in vHPC region, and increase negative changes in these brain regions including mPFC, BLA and NAc. CONCLUSION: Overexpression of Cofilin 1 in the vHPC CA1 subregion exerts antidepressant-like effects in mice, yet this intervention only ameliorates a subset of depression-related behavioral phenotypes. In contrast, knockdown of endogenous Cofilin 1 in vCA1 exacerbates OVX + CRS-induced dendritic and dendritic spine atrophy in the vCA1, and further aggravates adverse structural remodeling across downstream regions including the mPFC, BLA and NAc. Notably, these widespread neuronal morphological deficits triggered by vCA1 Cofilin 1 knockdown are insufficient to produce statistically significant worsening of depression-like behaviors in the model mice.

secondary.title: Disturbed Spatial Learning and Hippocampal Molecular and Histological Alterations in Middle-Aged Rats with a History of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Studies have reported inconsistent findings regarding the potential effects of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) on neurocognitive function. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate whether cognitive function, particularly spatial learning and memory, and hippocampal tissue are impaired in middle-aged rats with a history of PCOS. METHODS: Spatial learning and memory, hippocampal histopathology, and the expression of genes including beta-secretase 1 (bace1), microtubule-associated protein tau (mapt), amyloid-beta precursor protein (app), nestin (nes), and doublecortin (dcx) in hippocampal tissue were compared between middle-aged PCOS rats and controls (n = 7/group). RESULTS: During training (learning), middle-aged PCOS rats had significantly higher mean latency (22.04 (1.86, 42.22); P = 0.03) and duration (5.62 (1.41, 9.84); P = 0.009) than controls. However, memory performance did not differ significantly between PCOS rats and controls. PCOS rats had a significantly higher number of damaged neurons in the CA1 (24.25 ± 2.68 vs. 9.50 ± 0.64), CA2 (20.75 ± 1.03 vs. 8.25 ± 1.10), CA3 (20.50 ± 1.65 vs. 8.50 ± 1.04), and DG (28.25 ± 1.88 vs. 13.00 ± 1.29) regions of the hippocampus than controls (P < 0.05), and they showed mild hippocampal damage. In PCOS rats, bace1 gene expression was significantly increased in hippocampal tissue, whereas mapt gene expression was decreased compared with controls. The expression levels of the other genes did not differ significantly between the two groups. CONCLUSIONS: A history of PCOS during reproductive age may increase the risk of cognitive dysfunction, particularly impaired spatial learning, as well as hippocampal damage later in life.

secondary.title: SLC7A11-mediated dual regulation of disulfidptosis and ferroptosis in silver nanoparticles-induced neurotoxicity in hippocampal neurons.
secondary.abstract: Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) are widely used for their antimicrobial properties in consumer and biomedical products, prompting concern about their potential neurotoxicity. However, the mechanisms by which AgNPs drive neuronal death across different exposure durations remain poorly defined. In this study we investigated the temporal dynamics and mechanisms by which AgNPs induce neurotoxicity in hippocampal neurons, focusing on the cystine-glutamate antiporter solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11). Using combined in vivo (1-day acute and 28-day subacute intranasal exposure in mice) and in vitro (HT22 hippocampal neurons) models, together with inhibitors (deferoxamine, ferrostatin-1, TCEP), SLC7A11 siRNA, and surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) spectroscopy, we delineated a time-dependent switch between disulfidptosis and ferroptosis. Early (24 h) AgNPs exposure produced SLC7A11 up-regulation, cystine accumulation, NADPH depletion, GLUT1 down-regulation and F-actin collapse-features of disulfidptosis that were rescued by TCEP or SLC7A11 knockdown. With prolonged/subacute exposure, SLC7A11 and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) expression fell, iron homeostasis was disrupted, mitochondria showed ferroptotic morphology, hippocampal silver accumulated, and mice exhibited spatial memory deficits. SERS of AgNPs-cystine mixtures revealed cleavage of cystine disulfide bonds and formation of Ag-S complexes, a chemical transition that likely attenuates disulfide stress and facilitates the shift toward iron-dependent ferroptosis. Collectively, these data position SLC7A11 as a context-dependent metabolic switch governing the balance between disulfidptosis and ferroptosis, and provide a mechanistic basis to refine their safe and targeted application, particularly in biomedical contexts.

secondary.title: Perioperative Brain Damage Biomarkers Predict Neurodevelopmental Delay After Infant Cardiac Surgery: A Multicenter Study.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Infants with congenital heart disease are at high risk for neurodevelopmental impairment following cardiac surgery. Brain damage biomarkers may provide insight into perioperative brain injury and neurodevelopmental outcomes. METHODS: Prospective observational study conducted in two pediatric/neonatal cardiac intensive care units in North America and Europe in children undergoing cardiac surgery. Blood samples were obtained preoperatively and at 0, 24, 48, and 72 hours postoperatively to measure glial fibrillary acidic protein, ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1), neurofilament light (NFL), and microtubule-associated protein tau (TAU). Neurodevelopment was assessed at 2-years using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition, and a postoperative brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed. RESULTS: A total of 105 patients were evaluated by at least one study outcome modality (neurodevelopmental follow-up and/or brain MRI), including 61 patients with neurodevelopmental assessment. Despite differences in surgical complexity between centers, neurodevelopmental outcomes and MRI brain injury rates did not differ. All brain damage biomarkers showed dynamic perioperative changes. Brain injury was detected on MRI in 47.8% of patients but was not associated with outcomes. Higher perioperative NFL levels were associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes. NFL concentrations were increased in patients with cognitive delay (P = 0.01) and predicted cognitive and language delay (area under the curve = 0.65; 0.76, respectively). Patients with language and motor delay showed higher NFL levels (P = 0.04). UCH-L1 was associated with cognitive delay, whereas glial fibrillary acidic protein and total TAU were not associated with outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Elevated perioperative NFL levels were associated with and predictive of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, whereas UCH-L1 showed a weaker association with cognitive delay. Although MRI-detected brain injury was frequent, it was not associated with neurodevelopmental outcome.

secondary.title: Repurposing tirbanibulin as an orally active E2-targeting entry inhibitor against Chikungunya virus.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) causes severe acute and chronic disease, yet no approved specific antiviral treatment exists. To rapidly identify potential treatments, we aimed to screen an FDA-approved drug library for inhibitors of CHIKV infection. Tirbanibulin, a dual-microtubule polymerization and Src kinase inhibitor, was assessed for its potential anti-CHIKV activity. METHODS: We performed a high-throughput screen of an FDA-approved drug library. Mechanism-of-action studies included entry-step analysis, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) binding assays and molecular docking. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in lethal murine neuroinfection and CHIKV-induced arthritis models following oral administration of the candidate compound. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Tirbanibulin exhibited nanomolar to low-micromolar antiviral activity (EC50 range: 0.035-75.64 μM) across multiple cell lines, with high selective indices in key target HT22 and Huh7 cells. It acted at a post-attachment entry step, inhibiting clathrin-mediated endocytosis and potentially viral fusion. Surface plasmon resonance confirmed direct, high-affinity binding to the CHIKV E1 and E2 glycoprotein complex (K_D = 73 nM). In the lethal neuroinfection model, oral tirbanibulin significantly improved survival and reduced brain viral loads; in the arthritis model, it markedly attenuated footpad swelling and inflammatory pathology. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Tirbanibulin is a novel, orally bioavailable entry-stage inhibitor that directly targets the E2 glycoprotein. Multiple preclinical and clinical studies have confirmed its favourable oral bioavailability and safety. Given its established clinical safety profile, it represents a promising repurposing candidate for clinical evaluation against Chikungunya fever.

secondary.title: Multifunctional theranostic nanocarrier platform for microglia-selective cytochalasin D delivery to modulate neuroinflammation after acute brain injuries.
secondary.abstract: Targeting microglia to modulate neuroinflammation after acute brain injuries (ABIs) is promising but limited by poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration and systemic toxicity of candidate agents. In addition, multifunctional platforms combining targeted therapy with real-time traceability remain limited. We developed and characterized a multifunctional theranostic, folate-functionalized, polydopamine (PDA)-coated mesoporous silica nanoparticle (FA-NP) system for microglia-selective delivery and intracellular release of cytoskeleton inhibitor Cytochalasin D (CytoD). FA-NPs exhibited ideal physicochemical properties for parenchymal brain accumulation and pH-sensitive PDA shells enabled intracellular retention and gradual degradation. Using radiolabeled and fluorescein-isothiocyanate-functionalized FA-NPs, SPECT/CT imaging, γ-counting, autoradiography, and immunohistochemistry confirmed parenchymal brain accumulation with cellular uptake following systemic administration. Activated microglia upregulated folate receptors (FOLR1/2) and internalized FA-NPs via FOLR-mediated, dynamin-dependent endocytosis. CytoD-loaded FA-NPs (FA-NP[CytoD]) significantly reduced microglial migration, phagocytosis, ROS production, and proinflammatory cytokines, outperforming molecular CytoD while exhibiting notably lower toxicity compared to both CytoD and unfunctionalized particles. In organotypic brain slice models of hypoxia-reoxygenation and traumatic injury, FA-NP[CytoD] reduced inflammation at 24 and 96 h. Systemic administration enabled brain accumulation with clearance over time. Together, this multifunctional theranostic platform integrates selective microglial targeting, controlled drug release, and multimodal imaging, offering translational potential for ABIs.

secondary.title: Seasonal testicular regression in Yangzhou geese: Transcriptomic evidence for an immune-reproductive trade-off during the transition from peak to shutdown egg production.
secondary.abstract: This study investigated developmental changes and the underlying molecular mechanisms in testicular tissue of Yangzhou geese during the transition from the peak production (PP) to egg production shutdown (PF) periods. We hypothesized that this transition is accompanied by a reciprocal shift in resource allocation-declining spermatogenic activity offset by enhanced immune function-reflecting an adaptive life-history trade-off in this seasonally breeding species. Five Yangzhou geese were randomly selected each during the PP (day 73) and PF (day 135) periods, based on the endogenous seasonal reproductive rhythm of this breed under standard 12L:12D production lighting. Blood samples were collected for serum biochemical and hormonal analysis, and left testicular tissues were collected for RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) validation. The results show: the Johnsen spermatogenic score and the number of mature spermatozoa were significantly higher in the PP group (P < 0.05). Serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) concentration was significantly higher in the PP group than in the PF group (P < 0.05). RNA-seq identified 3605 DEGs (FDR <0.05, |log2FC| > 1); enrichment analysis (BH adj. P < 0.05) revealed significant upregulation of immune-related pathways (phagosome, hematopoietic cell lineage, complement and coagulation cascades) and downregulation of spermatogenesis-related terms (cilium movement, axonemal dynein complex assembly) in the PF group. Serum concentrations of interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and immunoglobulin G (IgG) were also significantly elevated in the PF group (P < 0.01), and immune indices were negatively correlated with reproductive indices. These findings support an adaptive immune-reproductive trade-off during seasonal testicular regression in Yangzhou geese, advancing our understanding of resource allocation strategies in seasonally breeding poultry.

secondary.title: Disruption of dopamine transmission by cholesterol depletion is associated with alterations in protein lipid raft partitioning and actin dynamics.
secondary.abstract: Disrupted brain cholesterol homeostasis is implicated in neurological disorders involving aberrant dopamine (DA) signaling; however, the direct effects of cholesterol on DA transmission in native tissue have not yet been demonstrated. Using ex vivo fast-scan cyclic voltammetry in nucleus accumbens slices from male rats, we found that membrane cholesterol depletion with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD, 3-10 mM) significantly reduced evoked DA release and decreased the apparent maximal rate of DA reuptake via the dopamine transporter (DAT). Because cholesterol is critical for the formation of lipid raft microdomains, cholesterol depletion could disrupt DA transmission by altering the membrane localization of proteins involved in neurotransmitter release. Using sucrose density gradient fractionation, we found that MβCD decreased the raft association of vesicle-associated membrane protein 2 (VAMP2) without altering the localization of syntaxin-1A, synaptosomal-associated protein 25, synaptotagmin-1, and N-type voltage-gated calcium channels. Therefore, MβCD may reduce DA release by disrupting localization of VAMP2, a core component of the vesicle fusion machinery. We also examined actin polymerization, a key regulator of vesicle docking and fusion, and found that MβCD treatment decreased actin polymerization, as evidenced by an increased globular-to-filamentous actin ratio and reduced phalloidin labeling of filamentous actin in striatal slices. Finally, although DAT lipid raft localization was unchanged, MβCD attenuated cocaine's ability to inhibit DAT reuptake function, suggesting that cholesterol depletion disrupts the outward-facing conformation of DAT required for high-affinity ligand binding. Overall, these findings provide new mechanistic insights into how cholesterol depletion may contribute to dysregulated DA signaling in diseases involving altered brain cholesterol metabolism.

secondary.title: Elevation of the mechanically-sensitive e protein emerin links nuclear mechanotransduction to tau-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in neurons.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, are neuropathologically defined by pathological tau deposition. While tau drives neurotoxicity by disrupting cytoskeletal, nucleoskeletal, and genomic architecture, cellular mechanisms mediating tau-induced dysfunction of the cytoskeleton and nucleoskeleton are incompletely understood. Here, we identify proteins with differing abundance in a cellular tauopathy model, iTau. Building upon previous findings that pathogenic tau reduces nuclear tension, we find elevated levels of emerin, a central regulator of nuclear mechanotransduction, in iTau neurons and tau mutant iPSC-derived neurons. Neuronal emerin overexpression drives neurotoxicity, increases filamentous actin (F-actin), and induces nuclear invagination, mimicking cellular phenotypes of tauopathy. Alterations in emerin binding partners reflect its cytosolic relocalization in iTau neurons, suggesting that pathogenic tau may impact nuclear mechanotransduction by altering emerin levels and localization. Overall, we identify emerin as a potential mediator of cytoskeletal and nucleoskeletal remodeling in tauopathy and provide a foundation for future studies of emerin function in neurons.

secondary.title: Adverse interactions of plastic nanoparticles with cultured primary microglial cells.
secondary.abstract: Due to ever-increasing production, plastics have become ubiquitous in the environment, with polystyrene (PS) being one of the most commonly produced types of plastics. Under the influence of mechanical pressure or UV radiation, plastic waste can decompose into smaller micro/nanoparticles (MPs/NPs), posing a threat to biological life, including humans. Recent findings indicate that MPs/NPs can penetrate biological barriers, including the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and affect cells of the central nervous system (CNS), including microglia, immune cells that play a key role in monitoring the neuronal microenvironment and responding to toxic compounds. The results of our study using primary microglial cells show that exposure to different concentrations (1, 25, 50 µg/mL) of polystyrene nanoparticles (PS-NPs; 25 nm) for different periods of time (24-48 h) results in a time- and concentration-dependent profile of NP internalization via an actin-dependent pathway. Once absorbed by cells, PS-NPs are directed to the endosomal-lysosomal system and induce cell activation, as evidenced by morphological changes (Sholl parameters) and increased levels of the Iba1 marker. The toxic effect of PS-NPs on primary microglia is expressed by reduced cell viability, overproduction of ROS and increased number of protein carbonyl groups induced by oxidative stress. These changes are accompanied by overexpression of pro-inflammatory chemokines, indicating activation of primary microglial cells towards a pro-inflammatory phenotype. The results suggest that PS-NPs may be a significant environmental risk factor leading to pro-inflammatory activation of microglia, which constitutes the first line of defense in the brain and is associated with the course of many neurological disorders.

primary.title: Female iPSC X chromosome inactivation erosion and its transcriptomic effects during CRISPR gene editing and neural differentiation.
primary.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders. Female iPSCs gradually lose the expression of the noncoding X chromosome inactive-specific transcript (XIST), leading to random X chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion that affects both X-linked and autosomal gene expression. However, the effects of CRISPR editing and neural differentiation on XCI erosion and how this may confound a real-world analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are poorly understood. Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data. We found variable XCI in CRISPR-edited female iPSCs, which was largely preserved in iPSC-derived neurons and predominantly influenced X-linked genes. Mechanistically, XIST mediates allele-specific epigenetic regulation of both X-linked and autosomal genes, with the former showing stronger allele-specific expression (ASE) bias that affects neurodevelopmental genes. These results have significant implications in hiPSC-based modeling of neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen reveals that Wnt signaling regulates lipid accumulation in APOE4 oligodendrocytes.
primary.abstract: APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, yet the cellular mechanisms linking APOE variants to disease risk remain unclear. We previously found that APOE4 expression causes lipid droplet accumulation in oligodendrocytes, reducing myelination, but the underlying mechanisms were unknown. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen and assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) sequencing in human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived oligodendrocytes, we identified decreased Wnt signaling and overactive glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B) as key regulators of lipid-droplet accumulation. Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of GSK3B reduced lipid droplets in APOE4 oligodendrocytes and increased myelination in three-dimensional iPSC-derived brain organoids. Pharmacological GSK3B inhibition also reduced lipid droplets and improved myelination in APOE4;PS19 tau transgenic mice. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework linking Wnt/GSK3B signaling to APOE4-driven disruptions in oligodendrocyte lipid metabolism and myelination, pointing to GSK3B as a potential therapeutic target for APOE4-associated Alzheimer's disease.

primary.title: An integrated human forebrain organoid reveals microglia-mediated CD8+ T cell recruitment and neuroimmune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease pathology.
primary.abstract: Genetic evidence implicates immune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the neuroimmune mechanisms operating in human tissue remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a modular human forebrain organoid platform that systematically integrates human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia and CD8+ T cells to reconstitute multicellular AD pathology. This system enables functional interrogation of both innate and adaptive immune components in a human-relevant context. Using this platform, we demonstrate that microglia mediate amyloid-β clearance and neuronal maturation but also drive inflammatory activation and recruit CD8+ T cells through CCL4/5 signaling via CCR1/5 and CXCR3, establishing a neuroinflammatory feedback loop. Pharmacological targeting of CCR5 or CXCR3 blocks T cell recruitment and modulates autophagy in a microglia-dependent manner. This modular organoid platform provides a versatile tool for dissecting neuron-immune interactions and enables cell-type-specific therapeutic screening in human neuroinflammatory disease models.

primary.title: The molecular footprint of valproic acid in human hippocampal organoid.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a multifaceted neurodevelopmental condition characterized by neuroinflammation, and disruption in neuronal development. Valproic acid (VPA) is a known environmental risk factor for ASD. Induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs IMR90-4)-derived human hippocampal organoids (hHOs) at 60 days of development were used to investigate VPA-induced changes in mRNA and microRNA (miRNA) profiles. The molecular effects of VPA on hHOs were deciphered by meaningfully integrating the ability of miRNA to regulate expression of their predicted mRNA targets crucial to altering neuroinflammatory pathways. Molecular footprint can be defined as the VPA-induced changes to the miRNA profile resulting in coordinated post-transcriptional (mRNA) regulation of neuronal and inflammatory pathways associated with ASD. Based on the results, the molecular footprint of VPA in hHOs was generated for the first time. These findings highlight the contribution of miRNA-mediated regulatory mRNA networks to VPA-induced neuroinflammation-associated with ASD in hHOs.

primary.title: MFN2-associated astrocyte dysfunction contributes to neuronal hyperexcitability and depressive-like behaviors.
primary.abstract: Astrocyte pathology is increasingly recognized as a key factor in the pathogenesis of major depressive disorder (MDD), where disrupted glutamate clearance and impaired neuron-glia interactions contribute to synaptic dysfunction. However, the molecular mechanisms leading to astrocyte loss remain largely undefined. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of MDD, yet most studies have focused on neuronal mitochondria, leaving astrocytic mitochondrial dynamics insufficiently investigated. Here, we identify mitofusin-2 (MFN2)-associated astrocyte dysfunction in depression. SMART-seq profiling of hippocampal astrocytes from chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) mice revealed Mfn2 up-regulation, accompanied by excessive mitochondrial fusion, impaired mitophagy, and astrocyte loss. Elevated MFN2 expression was detected in plasma, postmortem brain tissue, and iPSC-derived astrocytes from patients with MDD. Astrocyte-specific knockdown of Mfn2 restored mitochondrial morphology and mitophagy, thereby preserving astrocyte viability and alleviating depressive-like behaviors. Using mass spectrometry-based label-free proteomics, in vivo calcium imaging, and functional assays, we demonstrated that β-arrestin2 deficiency reduced STAT1 stability, releasing its transcriptional repression on Mfn2. Normalization of MFN2 expression through astrocytic Mfn2 knockdown or Stat1 overexpression reduced extracellular glutamate accumulation and prevented neuronal hyperexcitability in CSDS mice. Collectively, our findings define astrocytic MFN2-associated astrocyte dysfunction as a central pathological event in depressive behaviors, with the β-arrestin2-STAT1 pathway acting as an upstream regulatory mechanism. This work reveals an astrocytic pathway in depression and highlights a potential therapeutic target that directly addresses astrocyte pathology, beyond the neuron-centered focus of current antidepressant treatments.

primary.title: An aging-sensitive secreted phospholipase confers neuroprotection and cognitive resilience.
primary.abstract: Cognitive reserve theory posits that compensatory mechanisms during aging stave off cognitive decline and lower risk for Alzheimer's disease. Here, in a screen for hippocampal dentate granule cell (DGC) synapse loss-induced factors in mice, we identified a secreted phospholipase, Pla2g2f, whose expression increases in DGCs during aging and is associated with cognitive resilience in humans. Pla2g2f deletion in DGCs exacerbates aging-associated pathophysiological changes, including synapse loss, inflammatory microglia, reactive astrogliosis, impaired neurogenesis, lipid dysregulation, lipid droplet accumulation and hippocampal-dependent memory loss. Conversely, boosting Pla2g2f in DGCs during aging is sufficient to prevent these pathophysiological alterations in hippocampal-cortical circuits, protect memory and prophylactically modify trajectory of cognitive decline. Mutagenesis of the catalytic site of PLA2G2F prevented lipid droplet mobilization and reduction of reactive gliosis and inflammatory microglia. Neuronal PLA2G2F mediates intercellular signaling to decrease lipid droplet and cholesterol ester load in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Our findings implicate PLA2G2F as a compensatory neuroprotective broadcast signal that maintains lipid homeostasis to counteract aging-associated cognitive decline.

primary.title: APTX deficiency is associated with altered neuronal differentiation and alternative splicing in patient-derived neurons.
primary.abstract: Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia type 1 (AOA1), caused by mutations in the DNA repair protein aprataxin (APTX), leads to progressive neurodegeneration. In this study, we established an AOA1 patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) and a neuronal differentiation model. We demonstrated that AOA1-derived neurons exhibit neurite morphology and maturation defects correlated with the accumulation of DNA single-strand break (SSB) signals. AOA1-derived neurons showed greater DNA-damage and PAR signals together with lower protein-normalized NAD(H) and ATP after genotoxic exposure. These parallel changes are consistent with metabolic stress but do not establish a PARP1-dependent causal pathway. Bulk transcriptomic profiling and alternative splicing (AS) analysis further revealed widespread transcriptomic dysregulation and altered AS events, particularly enriched in neuronal genes essential for neurite development and synaptic function. Collectively, our findings identify neuronal differentiation, DNA-damage, metabolic, and transcriptomic differences in AOA1 patient-derived cultures and motivate composition-controlled and rescue-based studies of APTX function.

primary.title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

primary.title: PACS1 syndrome variant alters the proteomic landscape of developing cortical organoids.
primary.abstract: Patient-derived brain organoids have been used to model NDDs and identify pathogenic mechanisms. While most studies have evaluated the mechanisms by which NDD variants affect the transcriptome, studies examining the proteome remain limited. Here, we examined the effect of the PACS1 p.R203W variant, which causes PACS1 syndrome, on the proteomic landscape of brain organoids and compared the results with a transcriptomic dataset. Although we observed limited overlap between transcripts and proteins, most dysregulated processes converged. The proteomic data not only reinforced the importance of these developmental processes in p.R203W pathogenesis but also revealed dysregulated pathways not identified in the transcriptomic analysis. Key dysregulated transcripts and proteins in PACS1(+/R203W) organoids were classified as NDD-causative and ASD-risk genes. Our results highlight the potential of proteomics to complement transcriptomic studies by providing deeper insight into the mechanisms underlying NDDs while revealing additional therapeutic targets that may not be identifiable through transcriptomics alone.
